power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "However, ROI analysis revealed a significant negative association with fiber cross-section in the corpus callosum, with significant fixel clusters localized to the splenium (108 significant fixels; FWE-corrected p < 0.05; Figure 4A)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

text.text: Background: Children born preterm are at increased risk for attentional, social and emotional challenges, collectively referred to as the preterm behavioral phenotype.

While white matter alterations have been linked to individual behavioral domains following preterm birth, it remains unclear whether distinct dimensions of behavioral variability are associated with specific patterns of white matter organization.
Understanding neurobiological risk markers for preterm phenotypic traits may help identify children at greatest risk.

Objective: We investigated the extent to which these behavioral traits covary across the gestational age spectrum and whether latent behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter micro-and macro-structure in young children born preterm.

Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm ( 29females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks).
text.formatted: Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm ( <ref type="formula">29</ref>females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks).

text.text: Principal component analyses were performed separately in preterm, full-term, and combined groups to characterize latent behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning.
Fixel-based analysis was then used to examine associations between behavioral dimensions and fiber density and fiber cross-section, adjusting for demographic and perinatal factors.

Results: In the preterm sample, autism-and ADHD-related behaviors emerged as relatively distinct dimensions, whereas behavioral variance in the full-term sample was captured by a broad neurodevelopmental dimension.
In children born preterm, higher scores on the ADHD-related behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section in the splenium of the corpus callosum.
No significant associations were found for fiber density in the preterm or fullterm samples.

Conclusions: These findings suggest that prematurity influences not only behavioral outcomes, but also how those outcomes relate to white matter organization, highlighting the importance of considering behavioral heterogeneity when investigating brain-behavior relationships in preterm populations.
Preterm birth, defined as birth before 37 weeks of gestation, affects approximately 13 million infants worldwide each year (Ohuma et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Preterm birth, defined as birth before 37 weeks of gestation, affects approximately 13 million infants worldwide each year <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Ohuma et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Children born preterm experience a heightened risk of persistent neurodevelopmental difficulties, with the severity of this risk increasing with earlier gestational age at birth (Aarnoudse-Moens et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2020; Moore et al., 2012).

text.text: In addition to cognitive and motor challenges (Aarnoudse-Moens et al., 2009; Bhutta et al., 2002; Moore et al., 2012), children born preterm are two to three times more likely to develop autism (Crump et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2010), approximately three times more likely to develop attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Franz et al., 2018), and two to three times more likely to develop anxiety disorders (Fitzallen et al., 2021) than full-term peers.

text.text: Despite these group-level associations, developmental outcomes following preterm birth are remarkably heterogeneous (Burnett et al., 2011; Elgen et al., 2002; Mathewson et al., 2017).

text.text: This substantial variability underscores the need to identify predictive factors that may help explain why some children born preterm develop behavioral difficulties, whereas others do not.

Autism-related traits, attentional difficulties, and emotional symptoms have been consistently found to be elevated in children born preterm, leading Johnson and Marlow (2011) to propose the concept of the preterm behavioral phenotype.

text.text: This framework describes a characteristic pattern of attentional difficulties, autism-related social characteristics, and internalizing symptoms, often at subclinical levels (Fitzallen et al., 2020; Johnson & Marlow, 2011).

text.text: Although co-occurrence across these domains has been established in preterm populations (Fitzallen et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2010; Johnson & Marlow, 2011; Ritchie et al., 2015), datadriven profiling studies suggest that they are not uniformly co-elevated, with children born preterm exhibiting heterogeneous combinations and severities of behavioral difficulties (Burnett et al., 2019; Fitzallen et al., 2020; Lean et al., 2020).

text.text: Although autism-related, attentional, and emotional traits have been shown to covary in general-population samples (Gordon-Lipkin et al., 2018; Shakeshaft et al., 2023; Stergiakouli et al., 2017; van der Meer et al., 2017), it remains unclear whether and how preterm birth influences the organization of these relationships.

text.text: Characterizing the extent to which these traits covary may provide a more nuanced understanding of behavioral heterogeneity following preterm birth and a foundation for investigating the underlying neurobiological correlates of shared symptom dimensions.

The third trimester is characterized by rapid axonal growth, oligodendrocyte maturation, and the establishment of structural connectivity, making white matter particularly vulnerable to disruption following preterm birth (Back, 2017).

text.text: As white matter pathways support communication between distributed brain regions involved in attention (Hadaya et al., 2023; Vanes et al., 2021), social processing (Wang et al., 2018), and emotional regulation (Aarnoudse-Moens et al., 2009; Bhutta et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025), alterations in their development following preterm birth may contribute to the behavioral difficulties observed.

text.text: Several diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) studies have examined brain-behavior associations in children born preterm by investigating individual domains of behavioural functioning including autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, anxiety, or social functioning (Hosoki et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Loe et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2016).

text.text: Research using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), a common approach for modeling DWI data, has shown that attentional difficulties and internalizing symptoms are associated with altered white matter microstructure across multiple major tracts, including the corpus callosum, cingulum, superior and inferior longitudinal fasciculi, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, anterior thalamic radiation, and fornix (Loe et al., 2013).

text.text: In contrast, comparatively few studies have examined autism-related traits -although altered white matter microstructure in the left external capsule and superior fasciculus has been associated with higher overall autism screening scores (Skranes et al., 2007).

text.text: Most diffusion MRI studies have examined these behavioral domains separately, rather than considering their co-occurrence within children born preterm.

Consequently, despite some neuroimaging work beginning to use multivariate behavioral profiles to group individuals (Hadaya et al., 2023; Hadaya et al., 2025; Lean et al., 2020), relatively little is known about whether white matter organization relates to latent behavioral dimensions of the preterm behavioral phenotype.

text.text: Data-driven multivariate approaches can provide a means of characterizing this covariance by leveraging relationships across multiple behavioral domains to identify latent patterns of behavioral variability (Durham et al., 2023).

text.text: Several studies have adopted data-driven approaches (e.g., latent profile analysis) to characterize behavioral heterogeneity following preterm birth, identifying behavioral profiles characterized by elevated co-occurrence of ADHD, autism-related and anxiety symptoms (Burnett et al., 2019; Fitzallen et al., 2020; Lean et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Several studies have adopted data-driven approaches (e.g., latent profile analysis) to characterize behavioral heterogeneity following preterm birth, identifying behavioral profiles characterized by elevated co-occurrence of ADHD, autism-related and anxiety symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burnett et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fitzallen et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lean et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Some studies have further related these data-driven behavioral profiles to brain measures, including neonatal brain volumes (Lean et al., 2020) and functional connectivity (Hadaya et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Some studies have further related these data-driven behavioral profiles to brain measures, including neonatal brain volumes <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lean et al., 2020)</ref> and functional connectivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hadaya et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, these approaches characterize behavioral heterogeneity by assigning individuals to discrete profiles and examining neural differences between those groups.

Although this framework is valuable for identifying subgroups with similar behavioral presentations, it does not directly characterize how continuous patterns of covariation across behavioral domains relate to individual differences in brain structure.

In contrast, approaches such as principal component analysis (PCA) can characterize continuous patterns of covariation across behavioral measures, allowing individuals to vary along multiple behavioral dimensions.
Whether such continuous behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter organization following preterm birth remains unknown.

Early childhood provides a unique opportunity for investigating these relationships, as white matter continues to undergo substantial maturation during this period while differences in white matter development associated with preterm birth can persist beyond infancy (Kelly et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Early childhood provides a unique opportunity for investigating these relationships, as white matter continues to undergo substantial maturation during this period while differences in white matter development associated with preterm birth can persist beyond infancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kelly et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Concurrently, neurodevelopmental and behavioral difficulties become increasingly apparent during this age range.

To investigate these emerging brain-behavior relationships, we combined PCA with fixel-based analysis (FBA), which provides fiber-specific measures of white matter organization (Raffelt et al., 2017), in a sample of preterm and full-term children aged 4-8 years.

text.text: PCA was used to characterize continuous behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning, while FBA was used to examine whether these dimensions were associated with white matter fiber density and fiber cross-section after accounting for gestational age.

By integrating a dimensional behavioral framework with advanced diffusion MRI, we aimed to identify white matter markers associated with different dimensions of behavioral vulnerability following preterm birth and determine whether these brain-behavior relationships were specific to children born preterm or representative across the gestational age spectrum.

Data for the current study were collected as part of a longitudinal study investigating early childhood brain development in children born preterm. 83 children born preterm (42 females, < 37 weeks GA) and 137 children born full-term (79 females, ≥ 37 weeks gestational age) ages 4-8 were recruited into this study at the Alberta Children's Hospital, in Calgary, Canada. 25 preterm participants were recruited from the local Neonatal Follow-up Clinic, while other preterm and full-term children were recruited through community advertisements.
text.formatted: Data for the current study were collected as part of a longitudinal study investigating early childhood brain development in children born preterm. 83 children born preterm (42 females, < 37 weeks GA) and 137 children born full-term (79 females, ≥ 37 weeks gestational age) ages 4-8 were recruited into this study at the Alberta Children's Hospital, in Calgary, Canada. 25 preterm participants were recruited from the local Neonatal Follow-up Clinic, while other preterm and full-term children were recruited through community advertisements.

text.text: Participant visits included neuroimaging and behavioral and cognitive assessments.
All participants were screened for history of head trauma or any contraindications to MRI scanning.
Participants were excluded if they had seizure disorders, cerebral palsy, bilateral neurosensory hearing loss, and severe bilateral blindness.
Full-term participants additionally had no psychiatric or neurological diagnoses.
This study was approved by the Conjoint Health and Research Ethics Board at the University of Calgary.
Informed consent was obtained from the parents and informed assent from the participants.

After exclusions, the final sample included 58 preterm (29 females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; mean GA = 30.85 ± 4.20 weeks) and 85 full-term children (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks).

Exclusions were due to incomplete MRI acquisition (preterm N=2; full-term N=7), incomplete behavioral data acquisition (preterm N=10; full-term N=22), and poor-quality MRI data (preterm N=2; full-term N=7).
In addition, the original sample included 14 sibling or twin pairs (11 preterm pairs and 3 full-term pairs) and one full-term set of triplets.

Because the software used for FBA does not support modelling of random effects, only one child per family was retained in the final analyses, with the sibling exhibiting the least head motion during MRI acquisition selected for inclusion.
For preterm participants, demographic and perinatal information was collected using parent-or guardian-completed questionnaires.
Developmental information was collected from parents or guardians, supplemented by clinical chart review for children recruited through the Neonatal Follow-up Clinic.
For full-term participants, demographic and perinatal information was collected through parent report.

Behavioral assessments included the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) (Auyeung et al., 2008), the SNAP-IV 26 (Bussing et al., 2008), the Children's Alexithymia Measure (CAM) (Way et al., 2010), and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) (Crawford & Henry, 2004).
text.formatted: Behavioral assessments included the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Auyeung et al., 2008)</ref>, the SNAP-IV 26 <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bussing et al., 2008)</ref>, the Children's Alexithymia Measure (CAM) <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Way et al., 2010)</ref>, and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crawford & Henry, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The selected questionnaires assess behavioral domains commonly associated with preterm birth in pediatric populations, including autism-related traits, attentional difficulties, hyperactivity, and emotional dysregulation, with higher scores reflecting greater behavioral difficulties.
The AQ provides separate subscales indexing distinct autism-related characteristics, allowing assessment of trait-level variation across social, communication, and attentional domains.
We used scores from the attention switching (AQ-AttnSw), attention to detail (AQ-AttnDet), social skills (AQ-SS), imagination (AQ-image), and communication skills (AQ-Comms) subscales.
The SNAP-IV is a widely used and validated measure of ADHD-related symptoms that can separately quantify inattentive (SNAP-I) and hyperactive (SNAP-H) behaviors.
The CAM and PANAS capture emotional regulation and affective tendencies.
Only the negative affect component (PANAS-NA) of the PANAS was used, as it more specifically reflects emotional dysregulation and anxiety-related traits.
Participants completed two assessment sessions.
The first included developmental data collection, behavioral and cognitive assessments, and a mock scan.
The mock scan was designed to familiarize the child with the scanning environment, where they practiced remaining still while listening to simulated MRI scanner sounds.
Parents were advised to guide their child in practicing staying still at home before the actual MRI scan.
The second visit involved the collection of diffusion and structural MR images.
Participants chose a movie, show, or internet video to watch during the scan.
Strategies were used to minimize head motion, such as stabilizing foam pads.
MRI data was acquired on a 3T GE MR750w (Waukesha, WI) scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil.

Diffusion images were collected using a 2D spin-echo EPI sequence (two runs, one at b = 1000 s/mm² and one at b = 2000 s/mm², 45 diffusion-weighted directions, 3 non-DWI (b = 0 s/mm²), 23 × 23 cm FOV, 2.5 mm isotropic voxels, 45 slices, TR = 10 s, TE = 86.2 ms).
Structural T1-weighted images were also acquired using a T1-weighted 3D BRAVO sequence (24 × 24 cm FOV, 0.8 mm isotropic voxels, TI = 600 ms, flip angle = 10°).
Diffusion-weighted imaging data preprocessing was conducted using in-house scripts that employ routines from MRtrix3 (Tournier et al., 2019) and FSL (Andersson et al., 2016; Jenkinson et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Diffusion-weighted imaging data preprocessing was conducted using in-house scripts that employ routines from MRtrix3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Tournier et al., 2019)</ref> and FSL <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andersson et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Jenkinson et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: FSL's Eddy was used to correct for eddy current-induced distortion and head motion, as well as detection and replacement of slices with signal dropout.
DWI volumes with over 20% of slices with signal dropout were removed from the dataset.
If scans had more than 10% of volumes removed, they were excluded from analyses (resulting in the exclusion of 2 preterm scans and 4 full-term scans).

MRtrix3 was used to combine b=1000 s/mm² and b=2000 s/mm² shells, perform bias field correction using bias fields estimated from the mean b = 0 s/mm 2 images, and upsample all images to 1.25 mm³ to improve output contrast.

Intracranial volume (ICV) was estimated from structural T1-weighted images to account for age-related differences in head size that may influence morphological white matter metrics such as fiber cross-section.
Global ICV was generated using the FreeSurfer (version 7.1.1) reconall pipeline for tissue segmentation and estimation of tissue compartment volumes (Fischl, 2012).
text.formatted: Global ICV was generated using the FreeSurfer (version 7.1.1) reconall pipeline for tissue segmentation and estimation of tissue compartment volumes <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fischl, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: To obtain fixel-based metrics of fiber density and fiber cross-section, the MRtrix3 FBA pipeline was used.
A fixel represents a specific fiber population within a voxel, allowing multiple crossing fiber populations to be distinguished within the same voxel (Raffelt et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A fixel represents a specific fiber population within a voxel, allowing multiple crossing fiber populations to be distinguished within the same voxel <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Raffelt et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Fiber density reflects the intra-axonal volume of a fiber population, whereas fiber cross-section reflects the macroscopic cross-sectional size of the fiber bundle.
Each participant's scan was used to generate three-tissue response functions representing white matter, gray matter, and cerebrospinal fluid.

Response functions were averaged across participants to create a group response function, which was then used to perform multi-shell multi-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution (MSMT-CSD) to estimate white matter fiber orientation distributions (FOD).
Next, joint bias field correction and global intensity normalization of the multi-tissue compartments were conducted.
A FOD template was generated using data from 20 preterm and 20 full-term participants (matched for age and sex) that had good quality, low-motion scans.
This template was used to align all participants' FOD images, where they were then transformed into template space and segmented to estimate fixels.
Template fixels were used to mask each participant's fixels.
Following this, fiber density and fiber cross-section, which are expressed in arbitrary units, were computed.
Fiber cross-section values were log-transformed prior to statistical analysis, following the standard MRtrix3 FBA processing framework.
Connectivitybased fixel enhancement (CFE) was performed using MRtrix3's fixelcfestats to assess wholebrain fixel-wise associations.
Statistical inference was conducted using non-parametric permutation testing with family-wise error correction.

In addition, region-of-interest (ROI) analyses were performed within masks of tracts previously implicated in research examining preterm white matter injury and neurodevelopmental vulnerability (Kaur et al., 2025; Kelly et al., 2020; Pannek et al., 2018; Pecheva et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2024), including the corpus callosum (CC), corticospinal tract (CST), inferior longitudinal fasciculi (ILF) and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi (IFOF).
text.formatted: In addition, region-of-interest (ROI) analyses were performed within masks of tracts previously implicated in research examining preterm white matter injury and neurodevelopmental vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kaur et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kelly et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Pannek et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pecheva et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Zhou et al., 2024)</ref>, including the corpus callosum (CC), corticospinal tract (CST), inferior longitudinal fasciculi (ILF) and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi (IFOF).

text.text: Tracts of interest were delineated using TractSeg on the population template to generate tract orientation maps, where probabilistic tractography was conducted with 10 000 streamlines to produce tractograms.
From these tractograms, fixel maps were generated to create masks for the tract-specific fixel-wise analyses.

Differences in demographic characteristics between the preterm and full-term samples were assessed using independent-samples t-tests for continuous variables and Pearson's chisquare tests for categorical variables.
Group differences in behavioral measures were evaluated using Welch's independent-samples t-tests.
Differences in variance between the preterm and fullterm groups were assessed using Levene's tests.
To account for multiple comparisons across the nine behavioral measures, p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR).

The distinct principal component (PC) loading patterns identified across the three samples motivated separate examination of these behavioral dimensions in subsequent neuroimaging analyses.
The first two PCs were retained for subsequent analyses based on inspection of the scree plots, which demonstrated a clear elbow between the second and third components across analyses.

Together, the first two components collectively accounted for approximately 50-60% of the total variance, while subsequent components explained substantially smaller proportions of additional variance.
The interpretability of the corresponding loading patterns was also considered when determining component retention.

Spearman rank correlations were performed separately for the preterm and full-term groups to characterize relationships among the behavioral measures included in the PCA and to examine associations among demographic variables, perinatal variables, and principal component scores.

Associations between principal components and white matter metrics were tested using general linear models implemented in MRtrix3.
Fiber density and fiber cross-section were modeled separately for whole-brain fixel-wise analyses and tract-specific analyses.

Models included the relevant behavioral principal component as the predictor of interest and adjusted for age at scan, sex, gestational age at birth, birthweight adjusted for gestational age and sex, maternal education (a proxy for socioeconomic status), and days on mechanical ventilation (as a proxy measure for perinatal complication burden).
Maternal education was coded ordinally as0 = did not complete high school,1 = high school education,2 = college/trade school/diploma,3 = undergraduate degree, and4 = professional/graduate degree.

text.text: Within the preterm group, autism-related traits showed strong positive correlations among several AQ subscales (ρ = 0.59-0.77).
SNAP-I and SNAP-H scores were also strongly correlated (ρ = 0.73; Figure 2A).

text.text: In contrast, correlations between SNAP scores and AQ subscales were generally weak (|ρ| ≤ 0.23).

text.text: Within the full-term group, more consistent positive correlations were observed across ADHD, autism-related, and emotional measures (Figure 2B).

text.text: For example, AQ-CommS was moderately correlated with both SNAP-I (ρ = 0.52) and SNAP-H (ρ = 0.46), while CAM was moderately correlated with AQ-CommS (ρ = 0.59) and AQ-AttnSw (ρ = 0.46).
Direct statistical comparisons of corresponding correlation coefficients between groups supported several of these differences in cross-domain covariance.

The associations of AQ-CommS with both SNAP-I (PT: ρ = 0.06; FT: ρ = 0.52; z = -2.98, q = 0.033) and SNAP-H (PT: ρ = -0.01; FT: ρ = 0.46; z = -2.91, q = 0.033) were significantly stronger in the full-term group.

Similarly, CAM showed significantly stronger correlations with AQ-CommS (PT: ρ = 0.09; FT: ρ = 0.59; z = -3.22, q = 0.031) and AQ-AttnSw (PT: ρ = -0.01; FT: ρ = 0.46; z = -2.83, q = 0.033) in the full-term group.

Thus, despite showing generally lower variability in scores -which could be associated with lower correlations between scores through range restriction (Carretta & Ree, 2022) -the full-term group instead demonstrated greater correlations across behavioral domains whereas cross-domain associations were comparatively weak in the preterm group.

In the preterm-only sample, PC1 and PC2 explained 37.5% and 22.7% of the total variance, respectively (Figure 3A).

text.text: The loading structure demonstrated a clear separation between behavioral domains; PC1 was predominantly driven by autism-related traits, with strong positive loadings from the AQ subscales, whereas SNAP-I, SNAP-H, and CAM contributed primarily to PC2.
This pattern indicates that behavioral variability in the preterm sample was organized into relatively distinct dimensions reflecting autism-related and ADHD characteristics.
In the full-term only sample, the first two PCs explained 43.0% (PC1) and 14.8% (PC2) of the variance (Figure 3B).
text.formatted: In the full-term only sample, the first two PCs explained 43.0% (PC1) and 14.8% (PC2) of the variance (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3B</ref>).

text.text: PC1 was characterized by positive loadings on nearly all behavioral measures, consistent with a general behavioral dimension including autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional regulation.
PC2 included autism-and ADHD-related traits, with autism-related measures loading positively and ADHD/emotional regulation measures loading negatively.
However, compared with the preterm sample, autism-and ADHD-related measures exhibited greater overlap in PC1 and far less distinct separation across the first two components.
In the combined preterm and full-term sample, the first two PCs accounted for 38.5% (PC1) and 19.3% (PC2) of the variance (Figure 3C).
text.formatted: In the combined preterm and full-term sample, the first two PCs accounted for 38.5% (PC1) and 19.3% (PC2) of the variance (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3C</ref>).

text.text: PC1 represented a broad behavioral dimension, with autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional regulation measures all loading in the same direction, indicating that higher PC1 scores reflected greater overall expression of behavioral traits across domains.
In contrast, PC2 captured a differentiation in behavioral profiles with ADHD traits loading positively and autism-related traits loading negatively.
Thus, higher PC2 scores appear to reflect a behavioral profile characterized by relatively greater ADHD-related symptoms in relation to autism-related traits.

Spearman correlations among demographic variables, perinatal variables, and principal component scores were also examined to assess relationships between PCAderived behavior scores and predictors included in general linear models (Supplementary Figure S1).

text.text: Across all groups, principal component scores demonstrated generally weak correlations with demographic and perinatal variables.
In the preterm cohort, neither the autism-weighted (PC1) nor ADHD-weighted (PC2) dimension was significantly associated with gestational age or other perinatal variables.
These findings suggest that gestational age alone did not account for the observed behavioral variability within the preterm cohort.
No significant associations were observed between either the autism-weighted dimension (PC1) or the ADHD-weighted dimension (PC2) and fiber density in whole-brain or ROI analyses.
Likewise, no significant associations were observed between the autism-weighted dimension and fiber cross-section.
The ADHD-weighted dimension showed no significant associations in the whole-brain fiber cross-section analysis.

However, ROI analysis revealed a significant negative association with fiber cross-section in the corpus callosum, with significant fixel clusters localized to the splenium (108 significant fixels; FWE-corrected p < 0.05; Figure 4A).
text.formatted: However, ROI analysis revealed a significant negative association with fiber cross-section in the corpus callosum, with significant fixel clusters localized to the splenium (108 significant fixels; FWE-corrected p < 0.05; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4A</ref>).

text.text: Our findings suggest that higher expression of the ADHD-weighted dimension identified in children born preterm is associated with reduced fiber cross-section of the splenium of the corpus callosum.
No significant associations were observed between either PC1 or PC2 and fiber density or cross section at the whole-brain or ROI level in either the full-term only group or in the combined sample.
The present study characterized latent dimensions of behavioral traits in children born preterm and full-term and examined their associations with white matter fiber density and fiber cross-section.
Our findings suggest that the organization of behavioral variability differed between groups, with the preterm group exhibiting clearer separation between autism-related and ADHD-related dimensions.

Although fiber density is known to be altered following preterm birth, including in this sample (Kaur et al., 2025), neither of the behavioral dimensions identified within the preterm group were associated with fiber density.
text.formatted: Although fiber density is known to be altered following preterm birth, including in this sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kaur et al., 2025)</ref>, neither of the behavioral dimensions identified within the preterm group were associated with fiber density.

text.text: Higher scores on an ADHDweighted behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section within the splenium of the corpus callosum in the preterm group.

In the full-term group, the PCA revealed that autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional measures all loaded positively onto the first principal component, indicating that children with greater difficulties in one behavioral domain tended to exhibit greater difficulties across the others.

This pattern is broadly consistent with the general psychopathology ("p") factor described in dimensional models of psychopathology, in which diverse behavioral symptoms share a common source of variation and difficulties in one domain tend to accompany elevations across other domains (Caspi et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This pattern is broadly consistent with the general psychopathology ("p") factor described in dimensional models of psychopathology, in which diverse behavioral symptoms share a common source of variation and difficulties in one domain tend to accompany elevations across other domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Caspi et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A similar pattern emerged in our combined preterm and full-term analysis, where these behavioral domains also contributed in the same direction to a broad first component.

This finding is similar to recent work by Lean et al. (2026), who used PCA across full-term and very preterm children and identified a common parentreported component capturing shared variance across ADHD, internalizing, and social communication difficulties (Lean et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This finding is similar to recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Lean et al. (2026)</ref>, who used PCA across full-term and very preterm children and identified a common parentreported component capturing shared variance across ADHD, internalizing, and social communication difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lean et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, this pattern was not observed when PCA was performed separately within the preterm group.

Rather than contributing to a common behavioral dimension, autism-related traits and ADHD-related behaviors loaded onto distinct principal components, suggesting that although both may be higher in the preterm population on average, there is greater differentiation between those domains, as was also evident in pairwise correlations.

These findings suggest that while children born preterm can exhibit co-occurring behavioral difficulties, the organization and covariance of these traits may differ from that observed in children born full-term.
Thus, preterm birth may influence not only the overall burden of behavioral symptoms, but also the way these symptoms covary.
Together, these findings provided a rationale for allowing behavioral dimensions to emerge independently within each group rather than assuming a common behavioral structure across the full sample.

A consequence of this data-driven approach, however, is that the resulting components represented different behavioral constructs and limited our ability to compare brain-behavior across PT and FT groups.

Having identified distinct ADHD-weighted and autism-weighted dimensions within the preterm behavioral structure, we next examined whether individual variation along these dimensions was associated with white matter organization.

Neither preterm-derived behavioral dimension was significantly associated with gestational age, suggesting that behavioral variability within the preterm group was not simply related to degree of prematurity.
We found that higher scores on the ADHD-weighted principal component were associated with reduced fiber cross-section within the splenium of the corpus callosum.

The corpus callosum is among the white matter structures most consistently affected following preterm birth given its particular vulnerability to perinatal white matter injury (Jo et al., 2012; Malavolti et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The corpus callosum is among the white matter structures most consistently affected following preterm birth given its particular vulnerability to perinatal white matter injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jo et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Malavolti et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Zhou et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The splenium facilitates interhemispheric communication between posterior cortical regions involved in visuospatial, sensory, and higher-order cognitive processing (Blaauw & Meiners, 2020; Knyazeva, 2013).
text.formatted: The splenium facilitates interhemispheric communication between posterior cortical regions involved in visuospatial, sensory, and higher-order cognitive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Blaauw & Meiners, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Knyazeva, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, with this vulnerability, previous fixel-based studies have identified the splenium as particularly susceptible to the effects of prematurity, with reduced fiber cross-section associated with greater prematurity (Kelly et al., 2020; Pecheva et al., 2019), greater neonatal clinical risk (Kelly et al., 2020; Pecheva et al., 2019), and prolonged mechanical ventilation (Pecheva et al., 2019), as well as slower developmental increases in fiber density and fiber cross-section throughout childhood (Kelly et al., 2020).

text.text: Our previous work in this cohort similarly identified reduced fiber cross-section in the posterior corpus callosum with decreasing gestational age during early childhood (Kaur et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Our previous work in this cohort similarly identified reduced fiber cross-section in the posterior corpus callosum with decreasing gestational age during early childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kaur et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Abnormalities of the corpus callosum have also been associated with attentional difficulties and ADHD symptoms in children born preterm (Kim et al., 2023; Murray et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Abnormalities of the corpus callosum have also been associated with attentional difficulties and ADHD symptoms in children born preterm <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kim et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Murray et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that variation in splenial fiber cross-section may represent a neurobiological correlate of ADHDrelated behavioral variation in children born preterm, in addition to reflecting the broader vulnerability of this region to the effects of prematurity.
Interestingly, the ADHD-weighted dimension was not significantly associated with fiber density in the preterm group.

This should not be interpreted as evidence that splenium microstructure is unaffected in preterm birth, as previous neonatal and childhood fixel-based studies (including our own) have reported reductions in FD of the corpus callosum (Kaur et al., 2025; Kelly et al., 2020; Pannek et al., 2018; Pecheva et al., 2018).

text.text: Rather, our findings suggest that individual differences in ADHD-related behavior may be more closely linked to variability in white matter bundle cross-section than to fiber density during early childhood.

Fiber crosssection reflects the size and morphology of white matter fiber bundles and may provide information about the capacity of long-range interhemispheric communication that is complementary to that provided by fiber density (Dhollander et al., 2021; Raffelt et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Fiber crosssection reflects the size and morphology of white matter fiber bundles and may provide information about the capacity of long-range interhemispheric communication that is complementary to that provided by fiber density <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dhollander et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Raffelt et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Given the role of the corpus callosum in integrating distributed cortical networks (Wang et al., 2021), subtle alterations in bundle morphology may have functional implications for behavioral development.
text.formatted: Given the role of the corpus callosum in integrating distributed cortical networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Wang et al., 2021)</ref>, subtle alterations in bundle morphology may have functional implications for behavioral development.

text.text: Future longitudinal studies incorporating repeated behavioral and neuroimaging assessments are required to determine the relative contributions of microstructural and macrostructural white matter alterations to behavioural development across childhood.

Despite accounting for the largest proportion of behavioral variance in the preterm sample, the autism-weighted principal component was not significantly associated with either fiber density or fiber cross-section.

Together with the significant association observed for the ADHD-weighted dimension, these findings suggest that behavioral dimensions of the preterm phenotype may differ in the extent to which they are reflected in white matter organization.

The absence of significant associations with autism-related traits may indicate that variation in autism-related traits is influenced by neurobiological processes that are not captured by the white matter measures examined here.

Alternatively, autism-related behavioral variation may reflect the cumulative effect of subtle structural alterations distributed across multiple regions and tracts, rather than variation in a single white matter structure.

Thus, the lack of detectable associations with individual white matter measures does not necessarily imply an absence of neurobiological contributions to autism-related behavioral variation but may instead reflect the distributed nature of the underlying neural substrates.
This study has several strengths.
By using fixel-based analysis, we were able to characterize white matter micro-and macrostructure with greater sensitivity than conventional diffusion tensor imaging.
We also examined behavioral traits as continuous dimensions rather than categorical diagnoses, allowing patterns of covariation across behavioral domains to be captured.

Identifying these dimensions separately within preterm and full-term samples further allowed group-specific behavioral structure to emerge without assuming that the same latent dimensions applied across groups.

Additionally, our preterm sample spanned a broad gestational age range, which enabled investigation across the spectrum of prematurity, as much of the existing literature has focused primarily on very-and extremely preterm populations (Burnett et al., 2019; Hadaya et al., 2023; Hadaya et al., 2025; Lean et al., 2026; Lean et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Additionally, our preterm sample spanned a broad gestational age range, which enabled investigation across the spectrum of prematurity, as much of the existing literature has focused primarily on very-and extremely preterm populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burnett et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hadaya et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hadaya et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Lean et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lean et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We also acknowledge several limitations.
Firstly, behavioral measures were derived from parent-report questionnaires, which may be influenced by reporting bias and may not fully capture a child's behavioral variability.

Future studies could incorporate multiple informants, including parent, teacher, and child-report measures, alongside standardized behavioral or clinical assessments to provide a more comprehensive characterization of behavioral traits.

Secondly, although deriving behavioral dimensions separately allowed group-specific behavioral structure to emerge, the resulting differences in component structure prevented direct comparison of brain-behavior associations between the preterm and full-term groups.

Future multivariate work in larger independent preterm cohorts will be important to determine whether the observed separation of autism-and ADHD-related traits represents a reproducible feature of behavioral variation following preterm birth.
In addition, the cross-sectional design of this study prevents conclusions regarding developmental trajectories or the predictive value of these brain-behavior relationships.
Finally, although we examined the whole brain, our ROI analyses focused on tracts selected based on prior literature.
As a result, associations in other white matter regions may not have been detected.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that patterns of behavioral covariation in children born preterm may differ from those observed in children born full-term, with autism-and ADHD-related traits emerging as more differentiated dimensions within the preterm sample.

Specifically, reduced fiber cross-section within the splenium of the corpus callosum was associated with greater ADHD-related behavioral traits in children born preterm, highlighting a potential relationship between white matter macrostructure and behavioral variation during early childhood.

Together, these findings support the use of dimensional behavioral approaches and fiber-specific neuroimaging techniques to better characterize the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying behavioral heterogeneity following preterm birth.
Further characterization of these relationships in larger, longitudinal samples may ultimately improve understanding of individual differences in neurodevelopmental outcomes following preterm birth.
